title: Explain pass-by-value vs pass-by-reference — is Java pass-by-reference or pass-by-value, and why does passing an object reference confuse people?
shortTitle: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference, and why does passing an object reference confuse people?

s1_definition.profdef: Java is strictly pass-by-value. When you call a method, the argument's value is copied into the parameter. For primitives, the value copied is the primitive itself. For objects, the value copied is the reference, meaning the handle to the object, not the object itself. Because both the caller's variable and the parameter then hold copies of the same handle, they point to the same heap object, so mutations through the parameter are visible to the caller. But reassigning the parameter to a new object does not affect the caller's variable, which proves the reference was passed by value.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of an object reference as an account number written on a slip. When National Bank of India gives a method a copy of Rajesh's slip, the method has its own slip but it carries the same account number, so it reaches the same vault box and any change it makes to the box is seen by everyone. However, if the method scribbles a different account number onto its own slip, that only changes the method's copy; Rajesh's original slip still shows the old number. The method got a copy of the slip, not Rajesh's actual slip, which is why Java is pass-by-value even for objects.
s1_definition.oneliner: Java is always pass-by-value; for objects the value copied is the reference, so you can mutate the shared object but reassigning the parameter never changes the caller's variable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java is strictly pass-by-value. When you call a method, the argument's value is copied into the parameter. For primitives, the value copied is the primitive itself. For objects, the value copied is the reference, meaning the handle to the object, not the object itself. Because both the caller's variable and the parameter then hold copies of the same handle, they point to the same heap object, so mutations through the parameter are visible to the caller. But reassigning the parameter to a new object does not affect the caller's variable, which proves the reference was passed by value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of an object reference as an account number written on a slip. When National Bank of India gives a method a copy of Rajesh's slip, the method has its own slip but it carries the same account number, so it reaches the same vault box and any change it makes to the box is seen by everyone. However, if the method scribbles a different account number onto its own slip, that only changes the method's copy; Rajesh's original slip still shows the old number. The method got a copy of the slip, not Rajesh's actual slip, which is why Java is pass-by-value even for objects.

**One line to remember:** Java is always pass-by-value; for objects the value copied is the reference, so you can mutate the shared object but reassigning the parameter never changes the caller's variable.

sections.s2_technical:
Pass-by-value means the method receives a copy of the argument. Pass-by-reference would mean the method receives the caller's actual variable, so that reassigning the parameter would change the caller's variable. Java never does the latter; it always copies.

For a primitive, the copy is straightforward. If you pass an int and the method increments its parameter, the caller's int is unchanged, because the method only changed its own copy. For example a method that adds to a copied balance total has no effect on the caller's variable unless it returns the new value.

For an object, the value that gets copied is the reference, which is a handle to the heap object. So the caller's variable and the parameter are two separate handles that happen to point to the same object. If the method calls a mutating method on the parameter, like debit on an Account, it changes the shared object, and the caller sees that change because they point to the same object. This is the behavior people mistake for pass-by-reference.

The decisive test is reassignment. If the method does parameter equals new Account, it makes its own handle point to a brand-new object, but the caller's handle still points to the original. After the method returns, the caller sees no change, which proves the handle was a copy. The same applies to swapping: a method cannot swap two references for the caller, because it only swaps its own copies. A senior nuance is that this is exactly why defensive copying matters: if a method receives a mutable object and you do not want it mutated, you copy it inside, because the caller shares the same object. It also explains why String and other immutable types feel safe to pass; you cannot mutate them at all, so sharing the reference is harmless. Understanding this removes a whole class of bugs around unexpected shared-state mutation in a banking service.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at National Bank of India passed Rajesh's Account to a fee method, and the method debited a fee, and the caller was surprised the balance changed. They thought Java copied the object. This is exactly the object-reference confusion, because the method received a copy of the reference, not a copy of the object, so both pointed to the same Account and the debit was shared.

Problem 2 — Another developer tried to write a swap method to exchange two account references in the caller and found it did nothing. This is exactly the proof that Java is pass-by-value, because the method only swapped its own copies of the handles, leaving the caller's variables untouched.

In the mini-project we demonstrate all three behaviors. We define an `Account`, and a `ReferenceMechanics` class with a method that mutates a passed account (visible to caller), a method that reassigns its parameter (not visible), and a swap method (proves no pass-by-reference). The demo runs these on Rajesh and Priya and logs the before and after state so the reader sees exactly what changes and what does not.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/pbv/PassByValueDemo.java

# Run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.pbv.PassByValueDemo

# Expected: count stays 5; Rajesh debited (mutation visible); Priya unchanged
# after reassign; swap has no caller-side effect → proves pass-by-value
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a primitive count of 5, Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000), and Priya (CUR3001, 250000).

Step 1: incrementCopy receives a copy of the primitive 5 in its parameter. It increments its own copy to 6 and returns. The caller's count is a separate copy and remains 5, demonstrating pure pass-by-value for primitives.

Step 2: applyFee receives a copy of the reference to Rajesh's Account. Because the copy points to the same heap object, calling debit of 500 changes the shared object's balance to 999500. The caller reads 999500 afterward, which is the behavior people mistake for pass-by-reference but is simply mutation of a shared object.

Step 3: reassign receives a copy of the reference to Priya's Account. Inside, it points its own copy at a brand-new Ghost account. This only changes the method's local handle; the caller's priya variable still points to the original Priya object, so Priya's balance stays 250000, proving the reference itself was passed by value.

Step 4: swap receives copies of the references to Rajesh and Priya. It swaps its own two copies using a temporary variable, but the caller's rajesh and priya variables are untouched because the method never had access to them, only to copies. After swap, the caller's first variable still refers to Rajesh.

Step 5: The demo logs all four outcomes. The unchanged primitive, the visible mutation, the ineffective reassignment, and the ineffective swap together prove that Java is pass-by-value, and that for objects the value copied is the reference.

```text
[INFO] After incrementCopy, caller count still = 5
[INFO] After applyFee, Rajesh balance = Rs.999500
[INFO] After reassign, Priya balance = Rs.250000
[INFO] After swap attempt: first still Rajesh? true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  PRIMITIVE                          OBJECT REFERENCE
  caller: count=5                    caller: rajesh ──▶ Account(SAV2001)
    │ copy                             │ copy of HANDLE
    ▼                                  ▼
  method: n=5 → n=6                  method: account ──▶ same Account
  (caller count still 5)              ├─ account.debit(500) → shared obj changes ✓
                                      ├─ account = new Account(...) → only local handle moves ✗
                                      └─ swap(a,b) → swaps local copies only ✗

  Proof: reassign & swap have NO caller-side effect → pass-by-value.
  Confusion: mutation IS visible (same object), looks like by-reference.
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Defensive Copying in Account Service ═══

  ┌────────┐ REST ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ Client │─────▶│ Account Service      │
  └────────┘      │  service.applyFee(a) │  caller SHARES the object
                  │   → mutates shared a  │  (pass-by-value of reference)
                  │  service.quote(copy)  │  defensive copy when mutation
                  │   → copies before use │  must NOT leak to caller
                  └──────────┬───────────┘
                             ▼
                        PostgreSQL
  Rule: because references are copied (not objects), guard mutable
  inputs with defensive copies where caller must not see changes.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Pass-by-value mechanics ═══

  Argument type │ What is copied        │ Mutation visible? │ Reassign visible?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  primitive     │ the value             │ n/a               │ no
  object ref    │ the reference (handle)│ YES (same object) │ no

  ── Why confusion happens ──
  people see mutation flow back to caller and conclude "by reference",
  but it is mutation of ONE shared object via TWO copied handles.
  The reassign/swap test exposes the truth: handle was a COPY.

  ── Design implications ──
  defensive copy mutable inputs you must not alter
  immutable types (String, BigDecimal) safe to share freely
  return new values instead of mutating when purity is desired
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Java is strictly pass-by-value, always, with no exceptions. When I call a method, the argument's value is copied into the parameter. The subtlety is what the value is. For a primitive, the value copied is the primitive itself, so if the method changes its parameter, my original variable is untouched. For an object, the value copied is the reference, which is the handle to the heap object, not the object itself. So after the call, my variable and the parameter are two separate handles that happen to point to the same object.

That shared pointing is exactly why people get confused. If the method calls a mutating method on the parameter, like debit on an Account, it changes the one shared object, and because my variable points to that same object, I see the change. People look at that and conclude Java is pass-by-reference, but it is not; it is mutation of a single shared object reached through two copies of the same handle.

The decisive proof is reassignment. If the method points its parameter at a brand-new object, my original variable still points to the old object after the method returns, so I see no change, which could only happen if the handle was a copy. The same logic is why a swap method can never swap two references for the caller; it only swaps its own copies. In my banking work I use these facts constantly. When a fee method debits an Account I passed in, the change is visible because we share the object, and when a swap attempt does nothing, it confirms the handles were copied.

The practical design implication I always mention is defensive copying. Because the caller shares the same mutable object, if a method receives a mutable input that it must not alter from the caller's perspective, I copy it inside the method before working on it. This is also why immutable types like String and BigDecimal feel safe to pass around freely, since you cannot mutate them at all, so sharing the reference is harmless. So my complete answer is that Java is pass-by-value in every case, for objects the value copied is the reference so I can mutate the shared object and the caller sees it, but reassigning or swapping the parameter never affects the caller's variable, and that reassignment test is the clean proof that resolves the confusion.
